1184.title: Yoga (revisited)
1184.hook: follow any line of teachers back far enough and you meet a question: who taught the first one?
1184.howItsDone: In the Yoga Sutras, devotion to Ishvara is offered as one way toward stillness, and practitioners who follow it may repeat Om and reflect on its meaning, as the sutras describe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yoga's turn: follow a harmful thought to where it leads, and cultivate its opposite.

Who taught your teacher? It's a fair question in any craft. A violinist learned from someone, who learned from someone, who learned from someone else. The Samkhya Karika told its own chain: Kapila, then Asuri, then Panchashikha, and on down to Ishvarakrishna. Every link is a person who was once a beginner. But climb back up any line like that and you hit a strange question at the top. Who taught the first one? Patanjali's Yoga Sutras give an answer, and it's a clear place to see how Yoga parts ways with its closest neighbor.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOUR TEACHER?` → `THE CHAIN OF NAMES.` → `WHO TAUGHT THE FIRST?`

segments.voice: Ishvara came up three days ago in a single line, and in year two, verse by verse. Today we stay with it as the place Yoga and Samkhya part. Stillness can come, Patanjali says, through devotion to Ishvara, the Lord. Then he says who Ishvara is, in Samkhya's own vocabulary. Ishvara is a particular purusha, a witness like the others, but one never touched by the afflictions, by actions, by their ripening, or by the traces they leave. The Karika argued for many purushas, each seeming caught up in the world's show until the seeing is complete. Ishvara, in Yoga, is the one who was never caught. Then the line that answers the hook. Ishvara, the sutra says, is the teacher of even the earliest teachers, because Ishvara isn't limited by time. At the top of every chain of teachers, Yoga places one who never had to be a beginner. And Patanjali gives a way to reach toward him: his word is Om. Repeat it, the sutras say, and dwell on its meaning. Some readers call Yoga the Samkhya with Ishvara, and that's a fair label for the difference. Samkhya's count, as we heard it, had no place in the list for a Lord. Yoga keeps the list and adds one witness above the chain. Hindu tradition lets both schools stand side by side, and asks neither one to step down.
screen: `THE SAME MAP, A PRACTICE ADDED.` · `A PURUSHA NEVER CAUGHT.` · `TEACHER OF THE EARLIEST TEACHERS.` · `HIS WORD IS OM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that stuck, then the person who taught them, if you know, and let the line run back as far as it goes. Rest at the top of it, wherever that is for you. If you pray, you can say Om quietly a few times, as the sutras describe, and dwell on what it means to you.
Yoga. The school that keeps Samkhya's map and adds Ishvara, a purusha never caught, the teacher of even the earliest teachers.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. Every chain of teachers has a top, and Yoga names who stands there. Rest well.

1185.title: Yoga (revisited)
1185.hook: a brown line worn across a green lawn, and Vyasa's wheel of thoughts and traces
1185.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn Vyasa's picture of the wheel of turnings and traces, and teachers use it to explain why steady, repeated practice matters: each return of attention lays down a new trace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yoga's Ishvara: the purusha never caught, teacher of even the earliest teachers, whose word is Om.

Outside a library, a brown line runs across the lawn. Nobody planned it. There's a paved walkway around the corner, but someone once cut across the grass to save a few steps. Then someone else followed, because the grass was a little flatter there. Then everyone after. Now the line is bare dirt, and new feet take it without deciding to. The path made the walking, and the walking made the path. Vyasa's commentary on Yoga describes the mind working just like that lawn, and gives the loop a name.
screen: `A LINE ACROSS THE LAWN.` → `NOBODY PLANNED IT.` → `THE WALKING MAKES THE PATH.`

segments.voice: The name is samskara. In the Yoga Sutras it means the trace an experience leaves behind in the mind, like a footprint in grass. Patanjali's word for the mind's movements is vritti, a turning. Vyasa, commenting on the early sutras, ties the two together in a loop. Turnings leave traces, he says, and traces give rise to turnings again. And so the wheel of turnings and traces keeps going round, without pause. That's the lawn. A worry shows up, it leaves a groove, and the groove makes the next worry easier to have. In Yoga's account, that isn't a moral failing. It's how minds work. So what can be done about a path worn that deep? You can't argue a lawn out of its line. Here's the hopeful turn, near the end of the first chapter. Patanjali says that a trace born of true insight blocks the other traces. He means deep insight, not one good afternoon. But the principle carries: what wore the old path can wear a new one. Read in a small way, every time attention comes back to the breath, every time a sharp reply gets a second look, that's a footstep somewhere new. That's why Yoga cares so much about doing things again and again. Not because repetition is a virtue in itself, but because that's how a lawn changes. One more thing. Samskara has other homes in Hindu life. The same word names the rites that mark a life, from naming a child to a wedding. In Yoga, it means something quieter: the grooves underneath the next thought.
screen: `TURNINGS LEAVE TRACES.` · `TRACES MAKE TURNINGS.` · `A NEW TRACE BLOCKS THE OLD.` · `EVERY RETURN IS A FOOTSTEP.`

segments.voice: Rest attention on the breath in the belly, and let the mind wander down its old lines, the usual worry, the usual plan. Each time you notice, come back, and count, if anything, the returns rather than the wanderings: each one is a step across new grass. If you pray, you can let each return be a small offering.
Yoga. Vyasa's wheel: turnings leave traces and traces make turnings, and a trace of insight can block the old ones. Samskara is the trace.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. Every return to the breath is a footstep on new grass. Until tomorrow.

1186.title: Yoga (revisited)
1186.hook: one word on a studio window and on a battlefield: the many meanings of yoga before we leave the school
1186.howItsDone: Hindu traditions use the word yoga for many paths, including the yogas of action, knowledge and devotion in the Bhagavad Gita, while Patanjali's Yoga Sutras set out one systematic school of practice, in which posture is one limb among eight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yoga through Vyasa's wheel: turnings leave traces, traces make turnings, and a trace of insight can wear a new path.

The word is painted on a studio window downtown, above a stack of rolled mats. It's on a sticker on a water bottle. It's in the name of a phone app. And it's also spoken on a battlefield, in the Bhagavad Gita, by Krishna to a frightened prince who has let his bow fall. Same four letters. Is it the same thing? Before we leave Yoga as one of the six schools, a look at how wide the word really is.

Start with the studio. Patanjali does talk about posture. His word is asana, and what he says about it is short: the seat should be steady and comfortable. Effort relaxes, and the mind rests on the endless. There's no list of poses in the sutras. In Patanjali, posture is one limb among eight, a way of sitting still enough to look inward. Now the battlefield. In the Gita, Krishna uses the word again and again, and gives it different faces. Evenness of mind, he says, is called yoga: standing the same in success and failure. Two verses later: yoga is skill in action. And in the sixth chapter, a line with a twist: Krishna calls yoga the unjoining from sorrow, cutting the tie between a person and their pain. So which one is the real yoga? Hindu tradition doesn't make anyone choose. The Gita speaks of a yoga of action, a yoga of knowledge, a yoga of devotion. Patanjali's school is one careful, systematic version, with Samkhya's map underneath and Vyasa's commentary alongside. That's our time with Yoga, then. Samkhya's map, walked. Vyasa's five skies. Turning a harmful thought to its other side. Ishvara at the top of the chain. The wheel of traces. And a word wide enough to hold a quiet seat, a steady mind, a skillful hand and a heart cut loose from sorrow.
screen: `STEADY AND COMFORTABLE.` · `EVENNESS IS YOGA.` · `SKILL IN ACTION.` · `THE UNJOINING FROM SORROW.`

segments.voice: Shift until the posture is steady, not rigid, and comfortable, not slumped, and let effort loosen in the shoulders, the jaw, the hands. Then let the mind rest on something wide, the sky or the space around the body, coming back to the seat whenever a thought pulls. If you pray, you can rest in what you pray to as the wide thing.
Yoga. In Patanjali, a steady and comfortable seat on the way to stillness. In the Gita, evenness of mind, skill in action, and the unjoining from sorrow.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. One word holds a steady seat, an even mind and a skillful hand. I'll be here tomorrow.

1187.title: Mimamsa (ritual as meaning)
1187.hook: a recipe card that says add the cumin first, and a school that begins by asking what we're asked to do
1187.howItsDone: Mimamsa's study opens with the first of Jaimini's sutras, the desire to know dharma, and read the Veda's ritual passages as instructions, asking what each one asks to be done, and in what order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wide word yoga: a steady seat, evenness, skill in action, the unjoining from sorrow.

A recipe card, stained at one corner, in a grandmother's handwriting. Roast the cumin first. Then the onions. Never the other way. Nobody alive remembers why. Maybe it changes the flavor. Maybe it was just her habit. But the family keeps doing it, and the card keeps saying it. And sooner or later a grandchild holds the card up and asks the real question: is this telling us what to do, or just telling us a story about her kitchen? There's a school of Hindu thought built around that question, asked of the Veda. Its name is Mimamsa.
screen: `A STAINED RECIPE CARD.` → `CUMIN FIRST. ALWAYS.` → `A STORY, OR AN INSTRUCTION?`

segments.voice: The word Mimamsa can be translated as inquiry, or careful reflection. Its root text, the Mimamsa Sutras, is credited to the sage Jaimini, and its first line sets the whole program in a few words. Now, therefore, the desire to know dharma. Not the desire to know God, or the soul, or what the universe is made of. Dharma: what is to be done. Mimamsa looks at the Veda first as a body of instructions, and asks what it's asking of people. Above all, that means ritual: the fire offerings, the chants, the exact order of the steps. Here's what sets Mimamsa apart this season. Samkhya counted the world. Yoga trained the mind to see it clearly. Mimamsa says the meaning is in the doing. A ritual isn't a picture of a truth you could just think about instead. It's the thing itself, done right, at the right time, in the right order. Like cumin before onions. Now an echo. The Brahma Sutras, the root text of Vedanta, open with almost the same words: now, therefore, the desire to know brahman. Only the last word is different. Tradition pairs the two schools. Mimamsa is sometimes called the earlier inquiry, reading the Veda's ritual portions, and Vedanta the later inquiry, reading the Upanishads. Two schools reading one Veda, each with its own question. Mimamsa's is worth borrowing. Faced with an old habit, an old text, an old family rule: what, exactly, is this asking me to do?
screen: `THE DESIRE TO KNOW DHARMA.` · `THE MEANING IS IN THE DOING.` · `THE SAME OPENING, ONE WORD CHANGED.` · `WHAT IS THIS ASKING OF ME?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you do because it was handed to you: a way of greeting elders, a holiday dish, a prayer, a gesture. Without judging it, ask quietly what it asks you to do, and how exactly, then rest and let the doing itself be what you hold. If you pray, you can hold that practice in prayer.
Mimamsa. A school of careful inquiry into dharma, what is to be done, reading the Veda as instruction, where the meaning lives in the doing.
Your line: Mimamsa, ritual as meaning. Here, the meaning lives in the doing. See you tomorrow.

1188.title: Mimamsa (ritual as meaning)
1188.hook: a wedding video catches the fire, the steps and the vows, but no camera can film dharma
1188.howItsDone: Mimamsa teachers read the Veda's ritual lines as injunctions, the form 'one who desires this should do that', and hold that dharma is known through those words rather than through the senses or argument alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mimamsa began with the desire to know dharma, what is to be done.
screen: `THE DESIRE TO KNOW DHARMA.` · `HOW DO YOU KNOW IT?`

segments.voice: The wedding video is beautiful. Every angle is covered. The fire in the center, the priest's hands, the bride and groom walking around the flame, the rice, the garlands, an uncle crying in the second row. Play it back in slow motion and you can see every step. Now pause on any frame and point to the part that makes it right. The part that makes it dharma. You can't. The camera catches everything that happens, and misses what it means. Mimamsa takes up this problem in its second and fourth sutras.
screen: `THE WEDDING VIDEO.` → `EVERY STEP IN SLOW MOTION.` → `WHERE IS THE DHARMA?`

segments.voice: Jaimini's second sutra says what dharma is. In paraphrase: dharma is a good that is known through codana, the Veda's urging, its injunction. A command, in the plain sense: do this. Two sutras later, Jaimini explains why it has to be that way. Perception, he says, can't be the way to know dharma, because perception only grasps what's present to the senses right now. And dharma isn't sitting there in the present to be seen. Its good lies in what the act brings about, not in how it looks. That's the wedding video. The senses, like the camera, record what happens. They can't record what it's for. So where does Mimamsa find it? In the words that ask for it. The Veda says, in effect, the one who desires this should do that, and Mimamsa reads those lines with great care, as instruction. This changes how ritual looks. From outside, a rite can seem like a performance: steps, sounds, gestures. Mimamsa says the steps aren't decoration around a meaning. They're the answer to a call. The meaning of the act is that it was asked for, and that it's done. Other schools see this differently. Nyaya, which we met earlier this season, gives inference a large role alongside the Veda's word. Vedanta, at the end of this season, reads the Upanishads mainly as revealing what is, not only what to do. Mimamsa holds its own ground: some things can't be seen or proven. They can only be heard, and done.
screen: `DHARMA, KNOWN THROUGH INJUNCTION.` · `THE SENSES SEE ONLY THE PRESENT.` · `THE CAMERA MISSES WHAT IT'S FOR.` · `HEARD, AND DONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been asked to do and keep putting off: a call to return, a form to fill, a visit owed. Don't plan it; just hear the request plainly, as words, do this, and notice what happens in the body. If you pray, you can listen in prayer for what's being asked of you.
Mimamsa. The school that says dharma is known through the Veda's injunction, codana, because the senses only see what's present, and dharma lies in what the act is for.
Your line: Mimamsa, ritual as meaning. No camera can film what an act is for. Go gently.

1189.title: Mimamsa (ritual as meaning)
1189.hook: a letter drops into a mailbox and the act is over in a second, so how does the answer ever come back?
1189.howItsDone: Mimamsa teachers explain, following Shabara's commentary, that a properly performed rite produces an unseen potency, apurva, which persists after the act and brings its promised result in time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mimamsa said dharma is known through injunction, the Veda's do this, because no camera can film what an act is for.

The letter is stamped and sealed. A hand lifts the flap of a blue mailbox, lets go, and the flap clanks shut. The act of sending took about one second, and it's already over. And yet somewhere, in a bag, on a truck, in a sorting room nobody will ever see, the letter is still traveling. Weeks later, an answer arrives. So where was the sending, all that time? Mimamsa faced this exact puzzle about ritual, and gave its answer a name.
screen: `THE FLAP CLANKS SHUT.` → `THE ACT IS OVER.` → `THE ANSWER COMES LATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle. The Veda says, in effect, the one who desires heaven should perform this offering. Fine. The offering is done. The fire burns down, the chant ends, everyone goes home. The act is finished, gone. But the result it was for comes much later, maybe after this life. How can something that no longer exists bring anything about? Shabara, in his commentary on Jaimini's sutras, gives the answer. The act, he says, doesn't simply vanish. It produces something unseen, which stays and carries the act forward until its fruit arrives. Its name is apurva. Translators render it as the new thing, the unprecedented: something that wasn't there before the act, and is there after. Apurva is the letter in the bag. Notice what this does to ritual. An act done carefully today isn't wasted when it ends. Something has been set in motion that can't be filmed and can't be argued into being. It's known, Mimamsa says, only because the Veda asks for the act and promises its fruit. That fits yesterday. Dharma was something the senses couldn't see; apurva is how its good travels through time. Other Hindu schools speak of the lasting effect of action in their own ways, and the word karma covers a great deal of that ground. Mimamsa gave its own careful account, built for the fire and the offering.
screen: `THE ACT IS FINISHED.` · `THE FRUIT COMES LATER.` · `APURVA CARRIES IT.` · `THE LETTER IN THE BAG.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing you did that hasn't come back yet: a kind word, a gift, some care given without thanks. You don't have to know where it is now or what it will bring; with each out-breath, let the act be complete as an act. If you pray, you can offer it, as it is.
Mimamsa. In Shabara's account, a ritual act produces apurva, an unseen new thing that carries it forward until its fruit comes.
Your line: Mimamsa, ritual as meaning. The rite ends, and what it set moving travels on. That's today, done.

1190.title: Mimamsa (ritual as meaning)
1190.hook: a lullaby nobody remembers writing, and a school that says the Veda was never written by anyone
1190.howItsDone: Mimamsa holds that the bond between word and meaning is original and that the Veda is apaurusheya, not authored by any person, which is why its injunctions can be trusted as the means of knowing dharma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mimamsa's apurva: the rite is over, the fruit comes later, and something unseen carries it, like a letter in the bag.

A father hums a lullaby over a crib. His own mother sang it to him. Ask who wrote it, and he shrugs. Nobody wrote it. It was just always sung. Of course, somebody, somewhere, must have made it up first. We just lost the name. Mimamsa makes a much bolder claim about the Veda. Not that its author was forgotten. That it never had one. And a school so focused on doing has a reason to care who spoke the words.
screen: `A LULLABY OVER A CRIB.` → `NOBODY WROTE IT.` → `OR NOBODY EVER DID?`

segments.voice: Start with what Mimamsa needs. All week, its whole method has rested on one thing: dharma is known through the Veda's words, and nothing else can see it. So the words had better be reliable. If a person wrote them, a person could be wrong. Jaimini's answer comes in his fifth sutra. The bond between a word and its meaning, he says, is original. In Mimamsa's reading, nobody invented it. It's simply there. And so the Veda's instruction is a true means of knowing dharma, one that doesn't depend on anything else. Later Mimamsa thinkers spell out the consequence. The Veda is apaurusheya, not made by any person: heard and handed down, but never composed. Jaimini even meets an objection head on. Parts of the Veda are called after people, by names that sound like authors. Those names, he answers, come from the ones who taught and recited those parts, not from anyone who made them up. Here's why it matters to a school about ritual. If no one authored the words, then no one's mood, interest or mistake is hiding in them. The instruction can be trusted fully, and done fully. That's the week we've walked. Yoga set Ishvara at the top of the chain of teachers, and showed how traces wear a path. Mimamsa opened with the desire to know dharma, heard it in injunction, followed it through apurva, and now rests it on words with no author at all. Other schools hold other views of where the Veda comes from, and the tradition keeps all of them in the conversation.
screen: `THE WORDS MUST BE RELIABLE.` · `WORD AND MEANING, ORIGINAL.` · `NOT MADE BY ANY PERSON.` · `NAMES FROM TEACHERS, NOT AUTHORS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one line you were given, not one you made up: a blessing, a verse, a saying from home, a song. Let it play once, slowly, without analyzing it, then rest in the quiet after it. If you pray, you can let that line be your prayer.
Mimamsa. The school that holds the bond of word and meaning to be original, and the Veda to be apaurusheya, not made by any person.
Your line: Mimamsa, ritual as meaning. For Mimamsa, words no person made can be trusted fully. A week done, see you tomorrow.
